discovery: Metal-halide perovskite semiconductors for efficient photovoltaics and optoelectronics
motivation: Miyasaka first used metal-halide perovskites as photovoltaic absorbers in 2009. In 2012 Park made solid-state perovskite cells with long-term stability, and Snaith showed that the perovskite works as an ambipolar semiconductor in planar thin-film devices. Snaith's group also found that its charge-carrier diffusion lengths exceed a micron. Together these results revealed an unexpected class of solution-processed semiconductors whose physics behaves like that of the best crystalline materials. They have shallow defects, little non-radiative loss, sharp absorption edges and highly efficient luminescence. Power conversion efficiencies have since risen from 4% to above 27%, and perovskite-silicon tandem cells now exceed the single-junction silicon limit. These are the fastest gains in photovoltaic history, and they come with real mechanistic understanding, not just efficiency records. The materials have also opened new work on LEDs, detectors and defect tolerance in semiconductor physics. Industrial tandem modules are now being made. This discovery has changed what a whole field can make and understand.
